This is the fourth pre-release of Pudu. Its headline is derives: a type's equality, hashing,
ordering, display, JSON, and database rows are written once, as ordinary Pudu that reads the type's
shape while compiling. Programs also run markedly faster, and a sweep of the standard library
repaired many parsers and containers. The language and its tooling can still change before 1.0.

## Install

Download the archive for your machine, check it, and put its `bin` directory on your `PATH`:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c pudu-0.1.3-darwin-arm64.tar.gz.sha256
tar -xzf pudu-0.1.3-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
export PATH="$PWD/pudu-0.1.3-darwin-arm64/bin:$PATH"
pudu version
```

The standard library sits beside the executable inside the archive, so nothing is installed anywhere
else and deleting the directory removes Pudu. There are archives for Linux x86-64 and for macOS on
Apple silicon. Windows is not supported yet.

## Derives

```pudu
type Order = {
  @json("order_id") id: Int,
  lines: Array[Line],
  @skip cache: Option[Str],
} derives Eq, Hash, Json.Encode, Json.Decode
```

- `derives` on a record or sum asks for an implementation, and a `derive` declaration writes one
  once for every type: a `comptime for` over `Meta.fields[T]()` or `Meta.variants[T]()`, with
  `Meta.build` and `Meta.collect` to make values and arrays. Each derive is checked once, where it
  is written; it expands into an ordinary implementation before anything else is checked, so
  nothing about reflection reaches run time.
- `Std` ships `Eq`, `Hash` and `Ord` (with implementations for `Array` and `Option`), `Show`,
  `Json.Encode` and `Json.Decode` (honouring `@json(name)`, `@skip`, and `@default(value)`, with
  located decode errors), and `Db.Row` (honouring `@column(name)`). They work over records, sums,
  generic, recursive, and mutually recursive types. `Json` itself encodes and decodes, so a type can
  hold a JSON value.
- A field that cannot meet a derive is reported at the field:
  `Order.lines: Array[Line] does not implement Encode, which derive Encode requires of every field`.
- A derived JSON encoder runs as fast as a hand-written one, and a module with 400 types deriving six
  traits each checks in 1.5 s.
- `pudu expand <file>` prints the implementations a file's derives produce, as code its defining
  module could hold.
- A static member called through a generic parameter, `A.decode(json)`, now runs, whether the type
  is written or inferred.

## Faster programs

- Function bodies are compiled once to closures with locals in fixed slots, with the tree walker
  kept as the reference both are checked against. On the evaluator benchmarks at -O2, from 0.1.2 to
  now: an arithmetic loop 3.27 s → 0.55 s, record updates 2.57 s → 0.35 s, calls
  0.61 s → 0.27 s, and maps 1.22 s → 0.55 s.
- Text built with `+` is joined once when read: appending 320,000 pieces fell from 26.9 s to 0.5 s.
  Arrays sort natively (100,000 integers, 8.3 s → 1.6 s).
- `IntMap` and `IntSet` sit on the runtime's own map and set (80,000 mixed operations, 22.2 s →
  0.74 s), and the `MultiMap` benchmark runs in 0.67 s, from 8.15 s.

## The standard library

A layer-by-layer sweep repaired, among others: strict RFC 3339 and HTTP-date reading in
`Std.Time.Format`; YAML block and quoted scalars and nested compact sequences; JSON and TOML
numbers held to their grammars; Semver identifiers and `Accept` negotiation; URL ports, schemes,
and `+` in paths; HTML element and attribute names; marker reads in `Std.Net` and `Std.Tls` (a
32 MB head read, 8.99 s → under 0.3 s); `LinkedMap`, `LruCache`, `IntervalTree`, `Graph`, and
`PrefixTrie` costs; decimals compared numerically inside structures; and atomic file writes that
keep their permissions. `W3004` warns when a statement's value is dropped.

## Editors

- Inside `impl Trait for Type { }`, completion offers each trait member not yet written as a full
  method, and a quick fix writes every required one.
- Go to definition follows method calls — on a value, through a type, through a type parameter, or
  to an inherited default — and a derived method opens the derive that wrote it.
- Hover, definition, and completion work inside derive syntax: `derives` entries, `derive … for`
  headers, and a template's `field` and `variant`.
- A finding in an imported module appears at the import that reaches it, help is a line of its own,
  and notes such as `derive requested here` are links.
- The VS Code extension, 0.6.0, colours `derive`, `derives`, and attributes.
